Dec() produces the output in the requested format, e.g., a continuous embedding of the answer set, a discrete
set of entities, or a truth value. We note that the Encoder-Processor-Decoder framework is a conceptual
tool to analyze the existing approaches and is not a strict requirement for a model to have all three modules
explicitly. For instance, some models might not have a dedicated Processor module, or the Processor might
be merged with the Encoder or Decoder. We also note that the Encoder-Processor-Decoder framework is
not the only way to analyze the literature, but it is a convenient one.

5.1    Encoder

The Encoder module is responsible for building representations of the input query q, target graph G, and
auxiliary inputs in the latent space. The Encoder can be further decomposed into three sub-modules: (1)
Query Encoder, (2) Graph Encoder, and (3) Auxiliary Encoder. The Query Encoder builds a representation
of the input query q, the Graph Encoder builds representations of the target graph G, and the Auxiliary
Encoder builds representations of auxiliary inputs (e.g., node features, edge features, graph features). The
output of the Encoder is a set of representations that are passed to the Processor module.

Query Encoder. The Query Encoder builds a representation of the input query q. The query q is typically
represented as a graph (query graph) with nodes corresponding to entities, variables, and constants, and
edges corresponding to relations. The Query Encoder can be a simple lookup table (shallow embeddings)
or a more complex neural network (e.g., a GNN) that builds representations of the query graph. The
Query Encoder can also be conditioned on the target graph G (e.g., by using the same embedding space for
entities and relations). The Query Encoder can also be conditioned on auxiliary inputs (e.g., by using type
embeddings to enrich entity and relation representations).

Graph Encoder. The Graph Encoder builds representations of the target graph G. The Graph Encoder
can be a simple lookup table (shallow embeddings) or a more complex neural network (e.g., a GNN) that
builds representations of the entities and relations in the target graph. The Graph Encoder can also be
conditioned on auxiliary inputs (e.g., by using type embeddings to enrich entity and relation representations).

Auxiliary Encoder. The Auxiliary Encoder builds representations of auxiliary inputs (e.g., node features,
edge features, graph features). The Auxiliary Encoder can be a simple lookup table (shallow embeddings)
or a more complex neural network (e.g., a GNN) that builds representations of the auxiliary inputs. The
Auxiliary Encoder can also be conditioned on the target graph G (e.g., by using the same embedding space
for entities and relations).

5.2    Processor

The Processor module leverages the chosen inductive biases to process representations of the query with
its logical operators in the latent or symbolic space. The Processor can be further decomposed into two
sub-modules: (1) Logical Operator Processor, and (2) Graph Processor. The Logical Operator Processor
processes the logical operators of the query (e.g., conjunction, disjunction, negation, existential quantifica-
tion) in the latent or symbolic space. The Graph Processor processes the query graph against the target
graph G in the latent or symbolic space.

Logical Operator Processor. The Logical Operator Processor processes the logical operators of the
query (e.g., conjunction, disjunction, negation, existential quantification) in the latent or symbolic space.
The Logical Operator Processor can be a simple set of operations in the latent space (e.g., intersection,
union, complement) or a more complex neural network (e.g., a GNN) that processes the logical operators.
The Logical Operator Processor can also be conditioned on the target graph G (e.g., by using the same
embedding space for entities and relations).

Graph Processor. The Graph Processor processes the query graph against the target graph G in the
latent or symbolic space. The Graph Processor can be a simple set of operations in the latent space (e.g.,
graph traversal, message passing) or a more complex neural network (e.g., a GNN) that processes the query
graph against the target graph. The Graph Processor can also be conditioned on auxiliary inputs (e.g., by
using type embeddings to enrich entity and relation representations).

5.3    Decoder

The Decoder module produces the output in the requested format, e.g., a continuous embedding of the
answer set, a discrete set of entities, or a truth value. The Decoder can be further decomposed into two
sub-modules: (1) Answer Set Decoder, and (2) Truth Value Decoder. The Answer Set Decoder produces
a continuous embedding of the answer set or a discrete set of entities. The Truth Value Decoder produces
a truth value (e.g., a score) for a given query-answer pair.

Answer Set Decoder. The Answer Set Decoder produces a continuous embedding of the answer set or a
discrete set of entities. The Answer Set Decoder can be a simple set of operations in the latent space (e.g.,
nearest neighbor search) or a more complex neural network (e.g., a GNN) that produces the answer set.
The Answer Set Decoder can also be conditioned on the target graph G (e.g., by using the same embedding
space for entities and relations).

Truth Value Decoder. The Truth Value Decoder produces a truth value (e.g., a score) for a given
query-answer pair. The Truth Value Decoder can be a simple set of operations in the latent space (e.g.,
dot product) or a more complex neural network (e.g., a GNN) that produces the truth value. The Truth
Value Decoder can also be conditioned on the target graph G (e.g., by using the same embedding space for
entities and relations).

5.4    Summary

In this section, we discussed the literature from the perspective of Modeling. Following the common methodol-
ogy (Battaglia et al., 2018), we segmented the Modeling methods through the lens of Encoder-Processor-Decoder
modules (illustrated in Fig. 12). (1) The Encoder Enc() takes an input query q, target graph G with its
entities and relations, and auxiliary inputs (e.g., node, edge, graph features) to build their representations in
the latent space. (2) The Processor P leverages the chosen inductive biases to process representations of the
query with its logical operators in the latent or symbolic space. (3) The Decoder Dec() produces the output
in the requested format, e.g., a continuous embedding of the answer set, a discrete set of entities, or a truth
value. We note that the Encoder-Processor-Decoder framework is a conceptual tool to analyze the existing
approaches and is not a strict requirement for a model to have all three modules explicitly. For instance,
some models might not have a dedicated Processor module, or the Processor might be merged with the
Encoder or Decoder. We also note that the Encoder-Processor-Decoder framework is not the only way to
analyze the literature, but it is a convenient one.

5.5    Future Directions

The Encoder-Processor-Decoder framework provides a structured way to analyze and compare existing
approaches. Future work could explore the following directions:

*   **Unified Encoder-Processor-Decoder Architectures:** Developing unified architectures that seamlessly
    integrate the Encoder, Processor, and Decoder modules, potentially using a single neural network (e.g., a
    Transformer) to perform all three functions.
*   **More Expressive Processors:** Developing Processors that can handle more complex logical operators
    (e.g., negation, disjunction, existential quantification) and more complex graph structures (e.g., hypergraphs,
    multi-relational graphs).
*   **More Efficient Decoders:** Developing Decoders that can efficiently produce discrete answer sets from
    continuous embeddings, potentially using techniques like vector quantization or generative models.
*   **Incorporating Background Semantics:** Developing Encoders, Processors, and Decoders that can
    effectively incorporate background semantics (e.g., class hierarchies, complex axioms) to improve query
    answering performance.
*   **Theoretical Analysis:** Conducting theoretical analysis of the expressiveness and computational complexity
    of different Encoder-Processor-Decoder architectures.

6     Inference

In this section, we discuss the literature from the perspective of Inference. Inference refers to the process of
using a trained model to answer queries. We categorize the inference scenarios into three types: (1) Transductive
Inference, (2) Inductive Inference, and (3) Deductive Inference.

6.1    Transductive Inference

In transductive inference, the model is trained and evaluated on the same graph G. That is, all entities and
relations seen during training are also seen during inference. This is the most common inference scenario in
the literature.

6.2    Inductive Inference

In inductive inference, the model is trained on one graph Gtrain and evaluated on a different graph Gtest .
The graphs Gtrain and Gtest may have different sets of entities and relations. This is a more challenging
inference scenario that requires the model to generalize to unseen entities and relations.

6.3    Deductive Inference

In deductive inference, the model is trained on a graph G and an ontology O, and evaluated on the same
graph G and ontology O. The goal is to infer answers that are already implied by the graph G and ontology
O, but are not explicitly stated in the graph. This is a more challenging inference scenario that requires the
model to perform logical reasoning.

6.4    Summary

In this section, we discussed the literature from the perspective of Inference. We categorized the inference
scenarios into three types: (1) Transductive Inference, (2) Inductive Inference, and (3) Deductive Inference.
Transductive inference is the most common inference scenario in the literature. Inductive inference is a more
challenging inference scenario that requires the model to generalize to unseen entities and relations. Deductive
inference is a more challenging inference scenario that requires the model to perform logical reasoning.

6.5    Future Directions

The Inference perspective provides a structured way to analyze and compare existing approaches. Future
work could explore the following directions:

*   **More Robust Inductive Inference:** Developing models that are more robust to distribution shifts
    between the training and test graphs, potentially using techniques like domain adaptation or meta-learning.
*   **More Efficient Deductive Inference:** Developing models that can perform deductive inference more
    efficiently, potentially using techniques like knowledge distillation or approximate reasoning.
*   **Hybrid Inference:** Developing models that can perform a combination of transductive, inductive, and
    deductive inference, potentially using techniques like multi-task learning or transfer learning.
*   **Theoretical Analysis:** Conducting theoretical analysis of the generalization bounds and computational
    complexity of different inference scenarios.

7     Evaluation

In this section, we discuss the literature from the perspective of Evaluation. Evaluation refers to the process of
measuring the performance of a query answering model. We categorize the evaluation metrics into two types:
(1) Ranking Metrics, and (2) Classification Metrics.

7.1    Ranking Metrics

Ranking metrics measure the ability of a model to rank the correct answer(s) higher than the incorrect
answers. Common ranking metrics include:

*   **Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR):** The average of the reciprocal ranks of the first correct answer for
    each query.
*   **Hits@K:** The proportion of queries for which the correct answer is ranked in the top K.
*   **Mean Rank (MR):** The average rank of the first correct answer for each query.

7.2    Classification Metrics

Classification metrics measure the ability of a model to correctly classify whether a given entity is an answer
to a query. Common classification metrics include:

*   **Accuracy:** The proportion of correctly classified entities.
*   **Precision:** The proportion of entities classified as answers that are actually answers.
*   **Recall:** The proportion of actual answers that are correctly classified as answers.
*   **F1 Score:** The harmonic mean of precision and recall.

7.3    Summary

In this section, we discussed the literature from the perspective of Evaluation. We categorized the evaluation
metrics into two types: (1) Ranking Metrics, and (2) Classification Metrics. Ranking metrics are the most
common evaluation metrics in the literature. Classification metrics are less common but are used in some
works.

7.4    Future Directions

The Evaluation perspective provides a structured way to analyze and compare existing approaches. Future
work could explore the following directions:

*   **More Realistic Evaluation:** Developing more realistic evaluation benchmarks that better reflect
    real-world query answering scenarios, potentially using techniques like crowdsourcing or user studies.
*   **More Comprehensive Evaluation:** Developing more comprehensive evaluation metrics that capture
    different aspects of query answering performance, such as efficiency, robustness, and interpretability.
*   **Theoretical Analysis:** Conducting theoretical analysis of the properties of different evaluation metrics
    and their relationship to downstream task performance.

8     Conclusion

In this survey, we provided a comprehensive overview of the literature on complex query answering over
knowledge graphs. We introduced a unified framework for analyzing and comparing existing approaches based
on four perspectives: (1) Background Semantics, (2) Modeling, (3) Inference, and (4) Evaluation. For each
perspective, we discussed the key concepts, categorized the existing approaches, and identified future research
directions. We hope that this survey will serve as a useful resource for researchers and practitioners working
on complex query answering over knowledge graphs.
